title: Building My Mom's Bakery a Website in One Afternoon
creator: Marcus Webb
description:
Twenty-two years in business, zero websites. Fixed that in an afternoon.

Thanks to Pagecraft for sponsoring this video.

If you're ever in town: get there before 10, the cinnamon rolls sell out.

sentences.t: My mom has run a bakery in our town for twenty-two years, and she has never had a website.
Her entire online presence is a Facebook page that my cousin set up in 2014, and nobody knows the password to it.
So this weekend, I'm fixing that.
I've got one afternoon, a bunch of photos I took of her bread this morning, and a mom who keeps asking if this is going to cost her money.
Okay, first I sat down with her and asked what people actually need from the site.
Her answer was, my hours, my address, and that the cinnamon rolls sell out by ten.
Which honestly is a better brief than most clients give me.
So the plan is one page, with hours, location, a menu, and a gallery of the good stuff.
I'm building it in Pagecraft, and they're sponsoring this part of the video, so thanks to them.
I started from a blank page, not a template, because I wanted it to feel like her shop, not like every other bakery site.
First the header, I'm dragging in her logo, which I scanned off an old paper bag, and setting the background to this warm cream color from the shop walls.
For fonts, I picked a chunky serif for the headings, because her chalkboard menu has that hand-lettered feel.
Now the hours section, I'm adding a simple two-column block, days on the left, times on the right.
And here's a detail I love, I can set a little banner that only shows on Sundays, saying closed today, see you Monday.
Next, the menu.
Instead of typing it all out as a list, I'm using the grid, one card per item, with a photo, the name, and the price.
Sourdough loaf, six fifty, the famous cinnamon rolls, four dollars, and her seeded rye, which she insists be listed first.
Mom, it's alphabetical.
She said, it's my bakery.
So the seeded rye is first.
For the gallery, I'm dropping in about twenty photos, and it builds a masonry layout on its own, then I just drag the best ones to the top.
The map block takes the address and drops in a pin, and I'm putting it right next to the parking info, because parking on Main Street is a nightmare.
Then I check the phone preview, because I'd bet most of her customers look this up on their phone while standing outside.
The menu cards were a bit squished on mobile, so I switched them to a single column there, and now it reads nicely.
And finally, I connect her domain, which I bought last week as a surprise, and hit publish.
Okay, now the important part, the client review.
I handed her my laptop and just let her scroll.
She was quiet for a long time.
Then she said, the cinnamon rolls look smaller than they are.
That was the only note.
I'll take it.
Then she scrolled back up and read her hours out loud, like she was making sure they were real.
And I think she got a little emotional, though she will deny that.
Twenty-two years of people knocking on the door on Sundays, and now there's finally a place that says closed today, see you Monday.
She's already asked if we can add a page for birthday cakes.
So I guess I have another job.
If you've got a small business in your family that's still living on a Facebook page from 2014, this is your sign.
Thanks for watching, and if you're ever in town, get there before ten.
